title: Embedded Software Engineer
summary: Write, build, test and debug the software that runs on microcontrollers and small processors.
audience: Students who enjoy programming and want to work close to hardware.

sequence.why: C is the working language of the field; digital design and architecture explain what your code runs on.
Peripherals are how firmware touches the real world.
Almost every sensor and module is reached through one of these three buses.
Structure and tooling turn working demos into maintainable firmware.
Fast feedback is what separates hobby code from engineering.
Move from super-loops to scheduled tasks once the basics feel natural.

tools: VS Code or a vendor IDE

title: Embedded Hardware Engineer
summary: Design, prototype and validate the electronics that firmware runs on.
audience: Students who like circuits, soldering and understanding how boards work.

sequence.why: Everything else builds on circuit analysis and digital logic.
Hands-on measurement is how you learn to trust (or debug) a circuit.
Understand what the MCU needs to run reliably.
Hardware must expose the right buses and peripherals.
Layout and EMC knowledge turn a schematic into a real product.
Specialisations once the fundamentals are solid.

title: Firmware Developer
summary: Bring up boards and write the low-level code that talks to peripherals, bootloaders and buses.
audience: Students targeting bare-metal and driver-level work on microcontrollers.

sequence.why: Know the toolchain that turns C into a flash image.
These are the building blocks of every driver.
Reading sensors and storing data covers a large part of daily firmware work.
Firmware in the field has to recover, update and sip power.
Debug probes and simulators shorten the edit-test loop.

title: Embedded Linux Engineer
summary: Build, boot and extend Linux on single-board computers and custom hardware.
audience: Students who want to work with application processors, kernels and drivers.

sequence.why: The kernel is written in C and the shell is your daily tool.
Understand how a full Linux image is produced and started.
Kernel interfaces and process communication are core Linux skills.
Drivers sit on top of these buses.
UI, debugging and automation for shipping products.

title: IoT Developer
summary: Connect devices to networks and the cloud with secure, low-power communication.
audience: Students interested in connected devices, wireless links and data platforms.

sequence.why: Read sensors reliably before sending data anywhere.
Pick a radio based on range, power and data rate.
Lightweight messaging protocols are standard in IoT.
Battery life, updates and security decide whether a device is shippable.
Scheduling and on-device inference for smarter nodes.

tools: ESP32 or similar Wi-Fi / BLE board

title: Automotive Embedded Engineer
summary: Develop safety-critical ECU software and in-vehicle networks.
audience: Students aiming at ECU, ADAS or powertrain roles.

sequence.why: Automotive codebases are mostly C and C++ with strict style rules.
Deterministic timing is central to ECUs.
Know which bus is used for which domain of the vehicle.
Functional safety and structured processes are mandatory in the industry.
Control loops and secure communication for modern vehicles.

title: RTOS / Firmware Specialist
summary: Design multi-task, time-critical firmware on top of a real-time operating system.
audience: Firmware developers who want to specialise in scheduling, synchronisation and real-time behaviour.

sequence.why: An RTOS adds structure on top of these ideas; it does not replace them.
Tasks, scheduling, priorities and synchronisation are the vocabulary of RTOS design.
Compare designs and pick the one that fits the product.
Real-time systems fail at the boundary with hardware.
Tracing and testing concurrency bugs needs good tooling.
